question: What is the main goal of community mobilisation in primary health care?

options.A: Empowering locals to take charge of health

explanation: Community mobilisation focuses on enabling local populations to identify and solve their own health problems. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why is community participation critical for health interventions?

options.A: It eliminates the need for nurses
options.B: It stops all infectious diseases immediately
options.D: It reduces the cost of building hospitals

explanation: When people are involved in planning and executing health programs, they feel ownership, which keeps the initiatives alive over time. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is the very first thing a health worker must do during community entry?

options.A: Immunize all children under five years old
options.B: Build a modern primary health care clinic
options.C: Conduct a random drug trial in the village
options.D: Gain permission from traditional rulers and gatekeepers

explanation: Respecting local leadership through formal entry and greeting gatekeepers builds trust and opens doors for the healthcare team. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why is community profiling necessary before launching a health project?

options.A: It prevents outsiders from visiting the community
options.B: It automatically cures local malnutrition cases
options.C: It proves to the government that nurses are working hard
options.D: It reveals the unique demographics and culture of the area

explanation: Profiling gives health workers clear baseline data about who lives there and how they live, guiding appropriate planning. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of community sensitization?

options.A: To raise awareness and correct health misconceptions
options.B: To collect taxes from local market traders
options.D: To punish people who break sanitation laws

explanation: Sensitization aims to inform people about health risks and clear up wrong beliefs using culturally friendly communication methods. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h3)

question: A nurse planning a sensitization meeting in a rural village should use which method to reach the most people?

options.A: Academic lectures delivered in medical English
options.C: Town hall meetings and local drama in the native language
options.D: Written pamphlets distributed to university students

explanation: Using local languages and engaging formats like drama ensures that everyone, including those who cannot read, can understand the message. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h3)

question: Who should be targeted as key stakeholders during this step of mobilisation?

options.A: Foreign tourists visiting the local market
options.B: National politicians running for high office
options.D: Religious leaders, women's heads, and youth representatives

explanation: Local leaders hold immense influence over community behavior and are vital partners for driving health initiatives. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why is training community stakeholders so important for health programs?

options.A: It generates financial profit for local hospitals
options.B: It allows them to prescribe pharmaceutical drugs independently
options.C: It turns them into active advocates who champion the cause
options.D: It replaces the need for community health extension workers

explanation: Training empowers leaders with knowledge so they can guide their people and sustain the health program locally. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of priority setting in community mobilisation?

options.A: To make sure every single disease is treated on day one
options.B: To delay health interventions until funding runs out
options.C: To let health workers choose projects without community input
options.D: To focus resources on the most urgent health problem first

explanation: Since resources are limited, ranking problems helps the community tackle the most critical issue first. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which tool is best used during a participatory needs assessment?

options.A: Random guessing of local statistics by the nurse
options.B: Observing patients only inside the tertiary hospital
options.C: Focus group discussions with community members
options.D: Closed-door cabinet meetings in the capital city

explanation: Focus groups allow residents to openly discuss and share their actual lived health experiences and needs. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h5)

question: What does a community action plan typically include?

options.A: A list of punishments for community members who refuse care
options.B: Detailed medical histories of every nurse in the clinic
options.C: Financial statements of international donor agencies
options.D: Objectives, assigned tasks, timelines, and success indicators

explanation: An action plan provides a clear roadmap showing who will do what, when, and how success will be measured. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h6)

question: Why is it encouraged to use local resources during resource mobilisation?

options.A: It guarantees free medical supplies from the World Bank
options.B: It stops the community from working together
options.C: It builds self-reliance and reduces project dependency
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any planning

explanation: Using local resources ensures the community can sustain the project even if external donors pull out. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse during the implementation phase?

options.A: Taking over all physical labor so locals do not work
options.B: Writing laws to force people to attend health clinics
options.C: Sitting in an office away from the project site
options.D: Providing technical guidance and supporting community action

explanation: Nurses act as facilitators and technical guides while the community executes the planned health interventions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which factor is critical to maintain during the implementation of a health project?

options.A: Relying solely on commands from foreign experts
options.B: Excluding local leaders from daily operations
options.C: Strict secrecy about how funds and materials are spent
options.D: Transparency and clear communication among all participants

explanation: Open communication keeps everyone informed, builds trust, and prevents conflicts during project execution. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring tracks ongoing activities, while evaluation measures final impact
options.B: Monitoring costs money, while evaluation is always free
options.C: Monitoring happens after the project, while evaluation happens before
options.D: Monitoring is done by villagers, while evaluation is done by politicians

explanation: Monitoring happens continuously during the project to guide steps, while evaluation assesses overall results at the end. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h8)

question: Why should evaluation be participatory in community health projects?

options.A: it prevents the government from auditing the health center
options.B: It allows locals to assess their own progress and build capacity
options.C: It guarantees that no future health problems will occur
options.D: It ensures that nurses avoid blame if the project fails

explanation: Involving the community in evaluation builds local analytical skills and ensures true ownership of the project's outcomes. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T5#GNS124_U4_T5_h8)
